beats.say: Place a seed, turn by pi, repeat. You get seven spiral arms. Not three. Seven.
beats.speak: Place a seed, turn by pie, repeat. You get seven spiral arms. Not three. Seven.

head: THE RULE:
TURN, PLACE, REPEAT.
beats.say: The rule: place a seed, turn a fixed part of a circle, step out a little, repeat. Three hundred times.

head: HALF A TURN:
2 ARMS.
beats.say: Turn half a circle each time and you get two straight arms.

head: 2/5 OF A TURN:
5 ARMS.
beats.say: Two fifths of a turn: five arms. Any simple fraction makes straight arms. The bottom number is the arm count.

head: PI TURNS:
3 TURNS + 0.14159
beats.say: Now pi turns. Three full turns, plus 0.14159 of a turn. And that leftover is almost exactly one seventh.
beats.speak: Now pie turns. Three full turns, plus a little leftover. And that leftover is almost exactly one seventh.

head: 7 SEEDS =
21.99 TURNS.
beats.say: So after 7 seeds you have turned 21.99 times. Almost 22. Seed 8 lands right next to seed 1, and seven arms appear.
beats.speak: So after seven seeds you have turned almost exactly twenty two times. Seed eight lands right next to seed one, and seven arms appear.

head: MISSED BY
3.19 DEGREES.
beats.say: But not exactly. Every lap misses by 3.19 degrees, so each arm slowly bends into a spiral.
beats.speak: But not exactly. Every lap misses by just over three degrees, so each arm slowly bends into a spiral.

head: GOLDEN RATIO:
NO ARMS.
beats.say: Now the golden ratio, 0.618 of a turn. Mathematicians call it the most irrational angle. No fraction lines up. No arms, no gaps.
beats.speak: Now the golden ratio, about six tenths of a turn. People in math call it the most irrational angle. No fraction lines up. No arms, no gaps.

head: REAL SUNFLOWERS
USE THIS ONE.
beats.say: Real sunflowers pack like this. Count their spirals: 34 going one way, and 21 or 55 the other. Fibonacci numbers.
beats.speak: Real sunflowers pack like this. Count their spirals: thirty four going one way, and twenty one or fifty five the other. Fibonacci numbers.

beats.say: Pi flower or golden flower: which looks better? Comment.

title: Turn by pi and seeds make 7 arms. Turn by the golden ratio and they make none
caption: 300 seeds, one rule: place a seed, turn, step out, repeat. Half a turn gives 2 straight arms, 2/5 of a turn gives 5: with a simple fraction the bottom number is the arm count. Pi turns is 3 full turns plus 0.14159, almost exactly 1/7, so after 7 seeds you have turned 21.99 times and 7 arms appear. Each lap misses by 3.19 degrees, so the arms bend into spirals. The golden ratio, 0.618 of a turn, lines up with no simple fraction: no arms, no gaps. Real sunflowers count 34 spirals one way and 21 or 55 the other, all Fibonacci numbers.
notes: Seed i at radius c*sqrt(i+0.5), angle i*360*turn. Stats: pi_leftover 0.14159, one_seventh 0.142857, seven_pi_turns 21.99, seven_pi_miss_deg = 360*(22-7*pi) = 3.19, golden_turn = 1/phi = 0.618 (drawn as 137.508 deg, the same pattern mirrored). Science News (Ivars Peterson, Golden blossoms, pi flowers): pi seed angle about 0.14159 revolutions, roughly 50.97; for relatively small numbers of seeds seven spiral arms dominate; rational approximations of pi 22/7 and 355/113; golden 0.618 revolutions; if 34 rows curve one way there will be 21 or 55 the other; Fibonacci numbers. Knott (Surrey): p/q turns per seed gives q straight arms; 0.5 gives 2 arms; pi leftover 0.14159 close to 1/7 = 0.142857; pi shows 7 arms after 100 seeds. AMS Feature Column (Tony Phillips, The Most Irrational Number): plants place each seed at the most irrational angle possible, giving Fibonacci row counts. 300 seeds chosen so the 7 pi arms read clearly (checked on contact sheet). Constants: 2 and 5 arms for 1/2 and 2/5 (q arms rule), 7, 8 (seed after 7), 22 (nearest whole turns to 21.99), 21/34/55 (Science News). Series: 12 earlier posted visual lines in log.jsonl, so Math you can see #13 (12 + 1).
